claim: Patterns of intrinsic human brain activity exhibit a profile of functional connectivity that is associated with behaviour and cognitive performance.
source: Patterns of intrinsic human brain activity exhibit a profile of functional connectivity that is associated with behaviour and cognitive performance, and deteriorates with disease.
evidence: This is a general statement about functional connectivity supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Functional connectivity deteriorates with disease.
source: Patterns of intrinsic human brain activity exhibit a profile of functional connectivity that is associated with behaviour and cognitive performance, and deteriorates with disease.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Genes account for about 15% of the observed variance in fMRI connectivity.
source: On average over all connections, genes account for about 15% of the observed variance in fMRI connectivity (and about 10% in alpha-band and 20% in beta-band oscillatory power synchronisation), which substantially exceeds the contribution from the environment shared between twins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis on 820 subjects.

claim: Genes account for about 10% of the observed variance in alpha-band oscillatory power synchronisation.
source: On average over all connections, genes account for about 15% of the observed variance in fMRI connectivity (and about 10% in alpha-band and 20% in beta-band oscillatory power synchronisation), which substantially exceeds the contribution from the environment shared between twins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Genes account for about 20% of the observed variance in beta-band oscillatory power synchronisation.
source: On average over all connections, genes account for about 15% of the observed variance in fMRI connectivity (and about 10% in alpha-band and 20% in beta-band oscillatory power synchronisation), which substantially exceeds the contribution from the environment shared between twins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Genetic contribution to connectivity substantially exceeds the contribution from the environment shared between twins.
source: On average over all connections, genes account for about 15% of the observed variance in fMRI connectivity (and about 10% in alpha-band and 20% in beta-band oscillatory power synchronisation), which substantially exceeds the contribution from the environment shared between twins.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the variance decomposition analysis.

claim: Genes, rather than the developmental environment, have the dominant role in determining the coupling of neuronal activity.
source: Therefore, insofar as twins share a common upbringing, it appears that genes, rather than the developmental environment, have the dominant role in determining the coupling of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the comparative heritability analysis results.

claim: Spatially separated brain regions are organised into networks of strongly correlated activity during resting state.
source: Studying intrinsic activity, when the brain is in a resting state, has given insights into many aspects of healthy and diseased brain function. Resting-state function is characterised by spatially separated regions organised into networks of strongly correlated activity (Beckmann et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Resting-state networks represent both local connectivity and longer-range communication.
source: These networks represent both local connectivity and longer-range communication.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about resting-state networks.

claim: The strength of resting-state functional connectivity reflects many aspects of cognitive function.
source: Importantly, the strength of resting-state functional connectivity reflects many aspects of cognitive function.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Networks associated with attention and control may continue to develop in late adolescence.
source: Connectivity in the brain changes throughout the life cycle: networks associated with attention and control may continue to develop in late adolescence (Barnes et al., 2016) and network integrity degrades during the ageing process (Dennis and Thompson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barnes et al., 2016.

claim: Network integrity degrades during the ageing process.
source: Connectivity in the brain changes throughout the life cycle: networks associated with attention and control may continue to develop in late adolescence (Barnes et al., 2016) and network integrity degrades during the ageing process (Dennis and Thompson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dennis and Thompson, 2014.

claim: Schizophrenia has been associated with major alterations to the strength and organisation of functional connectivity.
source: Many neurological diseases, including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease (Sheline and Raichle, 2013; Greicius, 2008), have been associated with major alterations to the strength and organisation of functional connectivity (Stam and van Straaten, 2012; Stam, 2014; van Straaten and Stam, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Alzheimer's disease has been associated with major alterations to the strength and organisation of functional connectivity.
source: Many neurological diseases, including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease (Sheline and Raichle, 2013; Greicius, 2008), have been associated with major alterations to the strength and organisation of functional connectivity (Stam and van Straaten, 2012; Stam, 2014; van Straaten and Stam, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Intrinsic brain activity can predict performance in a task in healthy subjects.
source: In healthy subjects, intrinsic brain activity can predict not only performance in a task, but also the specific regions which will show increased activity during that task (Sala-Llonch et al., 2012; Yamashita et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013; Tavor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Intrinsic brain activity can predict the specific regions which will show increased activity during a task.
source: In healthy subjects, intrinsic brain activity can predict not only performance in a task, but also the specific regions which will show increased activity during that task (Sala-Llonch et al., 2012; Yamashita et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013; Tavor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The organisation of human brain function at rest is associated with a broad range of behavioural and life-style traits.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that the organisation of human brain function at rest is associated with a broad range of behavioural and life-style traits, and reflects a generalised measure of intelligence (Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2015.

claim: The organisation of human brain function at rest reflects a generalised measure of intelligence.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that the organisation of human brain function at rest is associated with a broad range of behavioural and life-style traits, and reflects a generalised measure of intelligence (Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2015.

claim: The study employed functional magnetic resonance imaging recordings from 820 subjects from the Human Connectome Project.
source: We employ resting-state recordings from 820 subjects from the Human Connectome Project (HCP; WU-Minn HCP Consortium et al., 2013); these data are publicly available, and have undergone a standardised pre-processing procedure.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: The HCP dataset includes 103 monozygotic twin pairs with fMRI resting-state scans.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This describes the composition of the study sample.

claim: The HCP dataset includes 54 dizygotic twin pairs with fMRI resting-state scans.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This describes the composition of the study sample.

claim: The HCP dataset includes 19 monozygotic twin pairs with MEG resting-state scans.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This describes the composition of the study sample.

claim: The HCP dataset includes 13 dizygotic twin pairs with MEG resting-state scans.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This describes the composition of the study sample.

claim: Monozygotic twins share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about monozygotic twins.

claim: Dizygotic twins share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
source: The HCP is a twin study, and the subjects from the S900 data release with all fMRI (MEG) resting-state scans comprise 103 (19) monozygotic twin pairs, who share 100% of their genetic structure and a common environment, and 54 (13) dizygotic twin pairs, who share 50% of their genetic structure and a common environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dizygotic twins.

claim: Each subject provided three MEG scans of 6 minutes each.
source: Each subject provided three MEG scans (of 6 minutes each), and four fMRI scans (of 15 minutes each).
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol.

claim: Each subject provided four fMRI scans of 15 minutes each.
source: Each subject provided three MEG scans (of 6 minutes each), and four fMRI scans (of 15 minutes each).
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol.

claim: Functional connectivity of two subjects becomes more alike as their proportion of shared background and genetics increases.
source: We compare the similarity in overall network structure between pairs of subjects, assessing the extent to which the functional connectivity of two subjects becomes more alike as their proportion of shared background and genetics increases.
evidence: This is a finding from the network similarity analysis.

claim: The fMRI connectome shows strong bilateral connectivity.
source: The fMRI connectome shows strong bilateral connectivity, together with fronto-parietal correlations and coupling between the anterior cingulate and posterior cingulate cortices, reflecting well-known patterns of resting-state networks in fMRI (Beckmann et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The fMRI connectome shows fronto-parietal correlations.
source: The fMRI connectome shows strong bilateral connectivity, together with fronto-parietal correlations and coupling between the anterior cingulate and posterior cingulate cortices, reflecting well-known patterns of resting-state networks in fMRI (Beckmann et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The fMRI connectome shows coupling between the anterior cingulate and posterior cingulate cortices.
source: The fMRI connectome shows strong bilateral connectivity, together with fronto-parietal correlations and coupling between the anterior cingulate and posterior cingulate cortices, reflecting well-known patterns of resting-state networks in fMRI (Beckmann et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the fMRI data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the MEG alpha band, the visual system shows strong connectivity.
source: In the MEG data, the alpha band shows a strongly connected visual system, with strong connectivity from the visual cortex extending out to the temporal and parietal lobes, and a highly coupled posterior cingulate.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG alpha band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the MEG alpha band, there is strong connectivity from the visual cortex extending to the temporal and parietal lobes.
source: In the MEG data, the alpha band shows a strongly connected visual system, with strong connectivity from the visual cortex extending out to the temporal and parietal lobes, and a highly coupled posterior cingulate.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG alpha band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the MEG alpha band, the posterior cingulate is highly coupled.
source: In the MEG data, the alpha band shows a strongly connected visual system, with strong connectivity from the visual cortex extending out to the temporal and parietal lobes, and a highly coupled posterior cingulate.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG alpha band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MEG beta-band exhibits strong bilateral coupling across the sensorimotor cortices.
source: The beta-band exhibits strong bilateral coupling across the sensorimotor cortices, with connectivity continuing through the superior parietal lobes and down to the occipital cortex.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG beta band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the MEG beta-band, connectivity continues through the superior parietal lobes and down to the occipital cortex.
source: The beta-band exhibits strong bilateral coupling across the sensorimotor cortices, with connectivity continuing through the superior parietal lobes and down to the occipital cortex.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG beta band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MEG theta band exhibits visual and motor connectivity.
source: The theta band also exhibits visual and motor connectivity.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the MEG theta band analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The observed patterns of MEG connectivity are in general agreement with previously reported results in these frequency bands.
source: These patterns of connectivity are in general agreement with previously reported results in these frequency bands (Hillebrand et al., 2012; Brookes et al., 2011; Baker et al., 2014; de Pasquale et al., 2012; de Pasquale et al., 2016; Hipp et al., 2012; Marzetti et al., 2013; Mantini et al., 2007; Colclough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Additive genetics accounted for 17%, on average, of the functional connectivity measured with fMRI.
source: Although there is a large amount of variability in the data which is not attributable to either of these factors, we found that additive genetics accounted for 17%, on average, of the functional connectivity measured with fMRI.
evidence: This is a finding from the variance component model analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In MEG, 19% of the variability in oscillatory coupling strengths in the beta band was determined by additive genetics.
source: In MEG, 19% of the variability in oscillatory coupling strengths in the beta band, and 8% in the alpha band, was determined by additive genetics.
evidence: This is a finding from the variance component model analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In MEG, 8% of the variability in oscillatory coupling strengths in the alpha band was determined by additive genetics.
source: In MEG, 19% of the variability in oscillatory coupling strengths in the beta band, and 8% in the alpha band, was determined by additive genetics.
evidence: This is a finding from the variance component model analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Using the 15-dimensional ICA decomposition, significant genetic influences were found in fMRI data with h²=0.29[0.26,0.33], p=1×10⁻⁴.
source: We found significant effects of additive genetic factors on the strength of inter-network connections in fMRI, using an alternative lower-dimensional parcellation based on 15 entire networks as nodes for the connectome. This suggests that genetic control of functional connectivity extends across multiple spatial scales of synchronisation. For oscillatory activity measured with MEG, it is not clear that it is meaningful to summarise, in the same manner as for an fMRI inter-network analysis, the collective behaviour of these gross network structures using a single time course: there is growing evidence from MEG that the extended networks from the fMRI literature are composed of smaller sub-networks that synchronise and de-synchronise on relatively fast time scales (Baker et al., 2014; de Pasquale et al., 2012; de Pasquale et al., 2016). That we found no significant genetic effects on the connections among this additional set of 15 networks in our MEG data may simply reflect the unsuitability of static whole-network parcellations for this modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the alternative parcellation analysis.

claim: No significant genetic effects were found for MEG connectivity using the 15-dimensional ICA parcellation.
source: We found significant effects of additive genetic factors on the strength of inter-network connections in fMRI, using an alternative lower-dimensional parcellation based on 15 entire networks as nodes for the connectome. This suggests that genetic control of functional connectivity extends across multiple spatial scales of synchronisation. For oscillatory activity measured with MEG, it is not clear that it is meaningful to summarise, in the same manner as for an fMRI inter-network analysis, the collective behaviour of these gross network structures using a single time course: there is growing evidence from MEG that the extended networks from the fMRI literature are composed of smaller sub-networks that synchronise and de-synchronise on relatively fast time scales (Baker et al., 2014; de Pasquale et al., 2012; de Pasquale et al., 2016). That we found no significant genetic effects on the connections among this additional set of 15 networks in our MEG data may simply reflect the unsuitability of static whole-network parcellations for this modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the alternative parcellation analysis with interpretation.

claim: Genetic control of functional connectivity extends across multiple spatial scales of synchronisation.
source: We found significant effects of additive genetic factors on the strength of inter-network connections in fMRI, using an alternative lower-dimensional parcellation based on 15 entire networks as nodes for the connectome. This suggests that genetic control of functional connectivity extends across multiple spatial scales of synchronisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding of genetic effects at both the focal ROI level and the inter-network level.

claim: No influence of genetic or environmental factors on MEG signal strength was found.
source: In our MEG data, we found no influence of these factors on the measured signal strength, and so can exclude this signal-to-noise effect as a likely confound in the beta-band MEG results.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of signal power shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was a significantly heritable component to signal power in the fMRI data.
source: There was a significantly heritable component to signal power in the fMRI data—but this is not surprising in and of itself.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of signal power shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cortical folding patterns have modest heritability.
source: Cortical folding patterns have been shown to have modest heritability (Sotiropoulos et al., 2015; Botteron et al., 2008; van Essen et al., 2014); although the strength of genetic control and the mechanism of influence are not yet certain (Tallinen et al., 2016; Gómez-Robles et al., 2015; Ronan and Fletcher, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical curvature exhibits the highest heritability around the sensorimotor areas and insula.
source: Cortical curvature exhibits the highest heritability around the sensorimotor areas and insula (as has been reported previously, in an analysis using a different sample of the HCP subjects; Sotiropoulos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the cortical curvature analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, supported by citation.

claim: The heritability of functional connectivity measured with electrophysiology has been reported before with heritabilities of 20–75%, predominantly in the alpha and beta bands.
source: The heritability of functional connectivity measured with electrophysiology has been reported before (Posthuma et al., 2005; Schutte et al., 2013; recording heritabilities of 20–75%, predominantly in the alpha and beta bands).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous electrophysiology heritability analyses were performed between EEG sensors using synchronisation likelihood, which is sensitive to volume conduction artefacts.
source: However, these analyses were performed between EEG sensors, using synchronisation likelihood for network estimation, a measure that is sensitive to volume conduction artefacts.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous methods based on knowledge of their limitations.

claim: The study uses a connectivity metric that explicitly suppresses volume conduction artefacts.
source: We use a connectivity metric that explicitly suppresses these artefacts (Colclough et al., 2015; Brookes et al., 2012; Hipp et al., 2012; O'Neill et al., 2015), reducing the influence of heritable anatomical features and cortical folding patterns on our results.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study supported by citations.

claim: No significant genetic control of functional connectivity was found in the theta frequency band.
source: We did not find significant genetic control of functional connectivity in the theta frequency band.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG theta band analysis.

claim: The lack of significant genetic control in theta band may be partly due to difficulty in cleanly estimating functional connectivity in MEG outside the alpha and beta bands.
source: This may be in part because of the difficulty in cleanly estimating functional connectivity in MEG, particularly outside the alpha and beta bands (Colclough et al., 2016), but may also be because the 89 HCP subjects with resting-state MEG scans present a much smaller sample for study than the rfMRI HCP dataset.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the null finding, supported by citation.

claim: The smaller MEG sample size (89 subjects) compared to the fMRI dataset may contribute to the lack of significant findings in theta band.
source: This may be in part because of the difficulty in cleanly estimating functional connectivity in MEG, particularly outside the alpha and beta bands (Colclough et al., 2016), but may also be because the 89 HCP subjects with resting-state MEG scans present a much smaller sample for study than the rfMRI HCP dataset.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the null finding.

claim: Structural connectivity is highly heritable.
source: Structural connectivity, the distribution of the white matter tracts across the brain that enable communication, is known to be highly heritable (Zhu et al., 2015; Jahanshad et al., 2012; Kochunov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A study of the heritability of structural connections with the HCP dataset estimated a mean heritability of 25%.
source: (A study of the heritability of structural connections with the HCP dataset estimated a mean heritability of 25%; Sotiropoulos et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous studies of the heritability of functional connectivity with fMRI find significant genetic effects with heritability estimates between 20% and 60%.
source: Previous studies of the heritability of functional connectivity with fMRI (which, in general, fail to control for subject motion, node power or brain size, and some of which focus instead on network topology), do also find significant genetic effects with heritability estimates lying between 20% and 60% (Smit et al., 2008; Fornito et al., 2011; van den Heuvel et al., 2013; Thompson et al., 2013; Jansen et al., 2015; Glahn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous fMRI heritability studies generally fail to control for subject motion, node power or brain size.
source: Previous studies of the heritability of functional connectivity with fMRI (which, in general, fail to control for subject motion, node power or brain size, and some of which focus instead on network topology), do also find significant genetic effects with heritability estimates lying between 20% and 60% (Smit et al., 2008; Fornito et al., 2011; van den Heuvel et al., 2013; Thompson et al., 2013; Jansen et al., 2015; Glahn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies based on review of their methods.

claim: Heritability estimates can change as network estimation methods improve because heritability is expressed as a fraction of observed phenotypic variance including measurement noise.
source: However, connectivity estimation is noisy, and as heritability is expressed as a fraction of the observed phenotypic variance (including measurement noise), we can expect the parameter estimates of heritability to change as network estimation methods improve.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of how heritability is calculated.

claim: Recent work has correlated profiles of gene expression in different cortical regions to resting-state fMRI connectivity profiles.
source: Recent work (Hawrylycz et al., 2015; IMAGEN consortium et al., 2015) has correlated the profiles of gene expression in different regions of cortex, and compared these patterns of gene transcription to resting-state fMRI connectivity profiles, identifying sets of genes with co-expression patterns that reflect networks of functional connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sets of genes with co-expression patterns that reflect networks of functional connectivity have been identified.
source: Recent work (Hawrylycz et al., 2015; IMAGEN consortium et al., 2015) has correlated the profiles of gene expression in different regions of cortex, and compared these patterns of gene transcription to resting-state fMRI connectivity profiles, identifying sets of genes with co-expression patterns that reflect networks of functional connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Functional connectivity profiles are associated with intelligence, which is well-known to be heritable.
source: Functional connectivity profiles are associated with intelligence, which is well-known to be heritable (Bartels et al., 2002; Neisser et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Connectivity is implicated with a broad range of behavioural and life-style factors including earning power, measures of health, various assessments of cognitive performance, and self-reported life satisfaction.
source: But connectivity is also implicated with a very broad range of behavioural and life-style factors, including earning power, measures of health, various assessments of cognitive performance, and self-reported life satisfaction (Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The environment in which individuals develop can make a significant impact on their performance and long-term outcomes.
source: As the findings of the Moving To Opportunity experiment in the United States make clear (Ludwig et al., 2013; Chetty et al., 2015), together with results from studies on the effects of schooling, socio-economic environment and adoption (Nisbett et al., 2012), the environment in which individuals develop can still make a significant impact on their performance and long-term outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nature, more so than nurture, is a major force in determining integrated cognitive function and cognitive capability.
source: However, while genes are not the only important factor, results such as these presented here suggest that nature, more so than nurture, is a major force in determining integrated cognitive function and, by extension, cognitive capability.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the study's findings about the relative importance of genetic versus environmental factors.

claim: All subjects in the study are young adults aged 22–35 years and healthy.
source: All subjects are young adults (22–35 years of age) and healthy.
evidence: This describes the study population.

claim: Resting-state fMRI data were acquired with 2 mm isotropic spatial resolution and a temporal resolution of 0.72 s.
source: Resting-state fMRI data were acquired with 2 mm isotropic spatial resolution and a temporal resolution of 0.72 s.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional connectivity was estimated among 39 functionally defined cortical regions of interest.
source: The functional connectivity measured with fMRI was estimated among 39 functionally defined cortical regions of interest (network nodes) by computing partial correlations between BOLD time courses representing each region.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: The parcellation contains contiguous regions identified from a resting-state 100-dimensional group-ICA decomposition of fMRI data from the first 200 subjects of the HCP project.
source: We used the parcellation employed in Colclough et al. (Colclough et al., 2015), which contains contiguous regions identified from a resting-state 100-dimensional group-ICA decomposition of fMRI data from the first 200 subjects of the HCP project.
evidence: This describes the parcellation method, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most ROIs have a symmetric counterpart in the opposite hemisphere, except those on the midline such as the posterior cingulate cortex.
source: Most ROIs have a symmetric counterpart in the opposite hemisphere, except those on the midline such as the posterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization of the parcellation.

claim: The low dimensionality of MEG data restricts parcellations to about 60 ROIs or less.
source: The low dimensionality of MEG data restricts us to parcellations of about this number of ROIs or less: as there are only a few hundred sensors, reconstructing time courses for more than approximately 60 different regions would be noisy or nonsensical.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of MEG.

claim: Models that categorise signals as originating within or without the MEG dewar suggest a limit of about 60 measurable cortical sources.
source: This upper bound is supported by models that categorise signals as originating within or without the MEG dewar, which suggest a limit of about 60 measurable cortical sources (Taulu et al., 2005), and by recently developed data-driven parcellations that only find around 70 unique identifiable parcels using combined MEG and EEG data (Farahibozorg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recently developed data-driven parcellations only find around 70 unique identifiable parcels using combined MEG and EEG data.
source: This upper bound is supported by models that categorise signals as originating within or without the MEG dewar, which suggest a limit of about 60 measurable cortical sources (Taulu et al., 2005), and by recently developed data-driven parcellations that only find around 70 unique identifiable parcels using combined MEG and EEG data (Farahibozorg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Resting-state MEG data were acquired on a whole-head Magnes 3600 scanner.
source: Resting-state MEG data were acquired on a whole-head Magnes 3600 scanner (4D Neuroimaging, San Diego, CA, USA).
evidence: This describes the MEG data acquisition equipment.

claim: MEG sensor-space data were down-sampled from 509 Hz to 300 Hz with the application of an anti-aliasing filter.
source: Sensor-space data were down-sampled from 509 Hz to 300 Hz, with the application of an anti-aliasing filter.
evidence: This describes the MEG data preprocessing.

claim: MEG data from each session were source-reconstructed using a scalar beamformer.
source: MEG data from each session were source-reconstructed using a scalar beamformer (Van Veen et al., 1997; Robinson and Vrba, 1999; Woolrich et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the MEG source reconstruction method with citations.

claim: A symmetric orthogonalisation procedure is used to compensate for spatial leakage confounds in source-localised MEG.
source: We compensate for these spatial leakage confounds, which can induce spurious connectivity estimates, using a symmetric orthogonalisation procedure (Colclough et al., 2015) to remove all shared signal at zero lag between the network nodes.
evidence: This describes the leakage correction method with citation, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The symmetric orthogonalisation procedure is a multivariate extension of the orthogonalisation principle proposed in Brookes et al., 2012; Hipp et al., 2012; and O'Neill et al., 2015.
source: This procedure is a multivariate extension of the orthogonalisation principle proposed in Brookes et al., 2012; Hipp et al., 2012; and O'Neill et al., 2015.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The orthogonalisation approach suppresses artificial correlations induced by spatial leakage at the expense of any zero-lag connections of true neuronal origin.
source: This approach suppresses any artificial correlations induced by spatial leakage, at the expense of any zero-lag connections of true neuronal origin.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the leakage correction method based on knowledge of how it works.

claim: Partial correlation used in fMRI data is one of the most accurate and robust measures in this modality.
source: Both are correlation measures, to maintain the similarity in analysis between the fMRI and MEG data. Partial correlation, used in the fMRI data, is one of the most accurate and robust measures in this modality (Smith et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013; Marrelec et al., 2006; Varoquaux and Craddock, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Regularised partial correlation is relatively unreliable in MEG.
source: An assessment of the repeatability of the most common network estimation measures in MEG showed that regularised partial correlation is relatively unreliable in this modality, and that the full correlation of the power envelopes of oscillatory activity (as we use here) was the most repeatable approach (Colclough et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Full correlation of the power envelopes of oscillatory activity is the most repeatable approach for MEG network estimation.
source: An assessment of the repeatability of the most common network estimation measures in MEG showed that regularised partial correlation is relatively unreliable in this modality, and that the full correlation of the power envelopes of oscillatory activity (as we use here) was the most repeatable approach (Colclough et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Repeating the fMRI analysis using full correlation rather than partial correlations yielded qualitatively similar results.
source: We did repeat our fMRI analysis using full correlation, rather than partial correlations, and found qualitatively similar results, with no difference in the significance of the claims we would make.
evidence: This is a finding from a sensitivity analysis.

claim: Similarity between pairs of functional networks was measured as the inverse Euclidean distance between correlation matrices after logarithmic projection onto a Euclidean plane.
source: Similarity between pairs of functional networks was measured as the inverse Euclidean distance between the correlation matrices, after a logarithmic projection onto a Euclidean plane locally tangent to the Riemann manifold of positive semi-definite matrices (Barachant et al., 2013; Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the network similarity metric with citations.

claim: The APACE system of permutation inference was employed for statistical testing.
source: The APACE system of permutation inference (Chen, 2014) was employed, using the mean network matrix (over resting-state recording sessions) for each subject.
evidence: This describes the statistical inference method with citation.

claim: The analysis regressed out effects of age, square of age, sex, age-sex interaction, sex-square of age interaction, cube root of intra-cranial volume, cube root of cortical volume, subject motion, and MR image reconstruction software version.
source: On each edge, we regressed out the effect of age, the square of age, sex, an age and sex interaction, an interaction between sex and the square of age, the cube root of intra-cranial volume and of cortical volume (both estimated with FreeSurfer), a measure of subject motion in the scanner (fMRI_motion) and, for the fMRI data, the MR image reconstruction software version.
evidence: This describes the confound regression approach.

claim: A regressor accounting for heritable changes in node power was included on each network edge.
source: On each network edge, we included a regressor to account for heritable changes in node power, computed as the geometric mean of the power in each of the two nodes that each connection joins.
evidence: This describes a confound control measure.

claim: A false discovery rate correction was applied to the 21 principal statistical tests conducted for this paper.
source: We applied a false discovery rate correction to the 21 principal statistical tests conducted for this paper to compensate for the multiple comparisons we perform (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction approach with citation.
